On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

When Computer Weekly launched in September 1966, computing was defined by mainframes, punch cards, and climate-controlled rooms that few people ever entered. By the time I was reading the publication early in my career, the world was on the brink of the dot com boom.

If you had told my younger self – a girl from County Cork, Ireland stepping into her first entry-level tech role – that technology would take me on a 30-year journey across global blue-chip companies, leading large transformations, and eventually serving as CTO of EMEA for Workday and a board director for Workday Limited, the idea would have seemed beyond reach.

Like many who joined the industry at such a pivotal time, I couldn't have mapped out that career trajectory. Over the last three decades, technology has given me the avenue to grow into what I believe I was born to be - a change-maker.

It also taught me that beneath every wave of technological evolution – from the emergence of dot com to cloud platform migration, and now to AI – the core story of technology has always been deeply human and built on trust.

My tech turning point

After initially serving on IT helpdesks, my first “tech epiphany” came at one of the General Electric businesses, where I stood up the company's first intranet in nine weeks. Moving away from localised server setups and processes layered with friction to web connectivity was a major turning point, showing me how technology could break down silos and transform a digital workplace to support employees.

By 2003 I was working for GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) during a stage of building, borrowing, buying and servicing tech to meet the growing demands across the business. I saw a change in attitude when it came to technology. No longer was it a case of “must we?” but a pivot towards “can we?”

In 2011 came another shift – cloud transformation – which turned out to be a defining moment in my career. Up to that point, HR was heavily reliant on legacy infrastructure and monolithic systems. GSK made the bold decision to become an early pioneer of enterprise software as a service (SaaS), selecting Workday to support its HR transformation globally. I led the IT deployment for the next couple of years, partnering with the business every step of the way.

It was uncharted territory, and stepping away from familiar legacy architecture and applications into a multi-tenant cloud model turned out to be both a challenge and a career gift.

By 2015, 120,000 employees across 135 countries were running on Workday HCM. For the first time, I wasn't just looking at uptime metrics behind a corporate firewall or managing resource- and time-intensive upgrades. I was watching in real time as employees across the globe interacted with software that actually made their working lives easier and more intuitive from day one.

“Tools will come and go, but the curiosity to learn, the willingness to adapt, the courage to be uncomfortable, and the commitment to solve real human problems will define the true technology change-makers”

Clare Hickie

I realised that software wasn’t just code complexity, technical elegance, or hardware specs. Software was - and is - about problem-solving. Specifically, solving real business and human challenges.

This moment changed the way I looked at both my role and the technology function. Software went from a back-office utility to a strategic necessity, and digital leaders finally gained a seat at the table. The change that enterprise software enabled inspired me so much that years later, when the opportunity surfaced, I took the chance and joined the software partner that drove that shift.

AI and the human imperative

Today, my days are spent in candid conversations with CIOs and digital leaders. When I sit with them, I recognise the challenges and opportunities they face. We’re living through another massive tech advancement with AI – as we did with the dot com boom and cloud migration – and the pace of change is faster than ever. It’s tempting to look back at tech history and focus on the internet or the iPhone, but AI is on another level. In 2,000 years of human history, this is the first time technology is taking on the role of a true teammate.

It is undeniable that AI is changing jobs and how we work. But look at our industry's history. When Computer Weekly printed its first issue in 1966, job titles like cloud architect, cyber security analyst, or data ethics lead sounded like science fiction. These shifts cause disruption, but that disruption frees us from low-level system admin so we can step into strategic, creative roles that previous generations couldn't have envisioned.

It’s why I speak so passionately to customers about augmenting human potential. When AI is deployed with a clear purpose, it doesn't displace human ingenuity. Today, purpose-built recruiting agents strip away repetitive admin tasks, like cutting candidate interview scheduling from weeks to hours. These time-savings show clear business value, but the real value comes when saved hours are reinvested - building genuine connections, understanding candidate potential, and defining future roles.

That transparency is essential because gaining workforce buy-in is only the first hurdle. Organisations face operational realities that can’t be glossed over – untangling legacy tech stacks, securing C-suite buy-in, and managing job redesign. But when employees have clarity on where the business is going and trust the destination, navigating those technical and financial challenges goes from a top-down push to a shared, achievable mission.

My lesson in leadership - lifting as you rise

Reflecting on this 60-year milestone for Computer Weekly, as well as my own 30-year tech journey, I am aware that I didn't reach this point through my own effort, passion and ambition alone. I was lifted up by mentors and sponsors – leaders who advocated for me when I wasn't in the room, and peers who showed me what excellence could look like.

Because of this, I feel a personal responsibility to throw the ladder back down for the next generation. Whether sponsoring our Women@Workday community, leading efforts with Connecting Women in Technology, participating in the T200, or championing our Future Females in Tech undergraduate initiative, my mission is to demystify technology careers, build clear pathways for the next wave of talent, and inspire anyone who is sparked by the wonders of technology – particularly those facing barriers to entry.

Matthew Syed captured it perfectly in his book Rebel ideas: “Collective intelligence emerges not just from the knowledge of individuals, but also from the differences between them.” Homogeneous engineering teams create blind spots, perpetuating bias in software design and AI models. When you bring together people with different backgrounds, perspectives, and lived experiences, you build superior, safer, and more innovative technology.

The future of innovation - curiosity and collaboration

Looking ahead to the next 60 years of business computing, the tools we use will continue to evolve at a rapid pace. The chatbots and large language models we champion today may eventually look as quaint to future generations as MS-DOS and floppy disks seem to some of us now. Believe it or not, back in my first helpdesk role, we used carbon paper to raise IT tickets.

Tools will come and go, but the curiosity to learn, the willingness to adapt, the courage to be uncomfortable, and the commitment to solve real human problems will define the true technology change-makers, just as it defined me.

Clare Hickie is CTO, EMEA at Workday.

title: Zopa Bank launches voice-controlled banking
raw_text:
Customers of Zopa Bank can now use voice commands to instruct an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered personal digital banking assistant to manage everyday banking tasks, such as making transactions or setting savings goals

The bank’s Ask Zopa feature understands and acts on instructions given by customers using conversational language, with the promise of removing additional manual processes.

The AI agent, which comes with the bank’s Biscuit account, can make payments for account holders, send money to their friends, and even calculate and pay a user contribution to a split bill. It “understands, remembers and personalises experiences”, said Zopa.

It can also make recommendations to people on reaching their financial goals through conversations.

Zopa, which pioneered peer-to-peer lending in 2005, closed that business in 2021, reinventing itself as a bank. It now has about two million customers and 300,000 holders of its Biscuit current account, which it launched last year.

Ask Zopa, which was built on the bank’s proprietary AI platform and agentic architecture on top of publicly available models, is the latest addition to the Biscuit account. The feature has been trialled with selected customers, but is now available to all those with a current account.

Clare Gambardella, chief customer officer at Zopa Bank, said the AI agent will remove more manual processes: “It will help customers manage and automate their finances, complete day-to-day banking tasks, and plan and optimise for the future.”

She said it can “execute on tasks in the app” and “give information or perspective”, all through the medium of voice, or text if preferred.

“Because it has context and can see as much information as you want it to, in terms of connecting accounts or other things, it can start to give a helpful perspective on how to meet, for example, a savings goal.”

Zopa recently added more tech know-how to its board with the appointment of Paula Walter, former Aldermore Group chief technology and information officer, as an independent non-executive director.

“Her experience managing considerable budgets and working with regulated entities is really going to be an addition for our board as we look forward to scaling Zopa even further,” said the bank.

Walter said: “Zopa has a clear ambition to make money management simpler and better for customers, underpinned by an impressive technology platform and culture. I’m excited to join the board and help the business continue to innovate responsibly, strengthen its resilience and deliver exceptional customer experiences at even greater scale, supported by AI-led change and innovation.”

AI is driving cost savings, as well as improving customer service at banks. Last year, Zopa released the findings of a survey carried out with Juniper Research, which revealed that UK banks will save £1.8bn over the next five years as a result of investing the same amount in AI.

The survey found that 187 million hours will be saved, mainly as a result of back-office efficiencies.

Last year, Zopa announced its plan to upskill and reskill 100,000 banking professionals in AI disciplines by 2030, through an industry coalition. The initiative launched in May this year, after 22 partners signed up.

The five-year Jobs2030 campaign offers modules in AI disciplines for fintech workers, specifically engineers, analysts and operations leads. Participants receive training tailored to the UK banking sector.

title: Cisco users urged to patch email gateway flaw
raw_text:
Cisco is urging defenders to get out in front of a highlydangerous flaw in its Secure Email Gateway (SEG) appliance, CVE-2026-76461, that could enable an unauthenticated, remote attacker to gain the ability to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges.

Listed on the US’ Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (Cisa’s) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (Kev) catalogue as of Monday 14 September, CVE-2026-76461 arises in SEG’s underlying AsyncOS software and occurs due to insufficient validation in the email parsing logic.

In simple terms, an attacker could exploit this by sending an email containing malicious Structured Query Language (SQL) statements via an affected device, Cisco explained. It was uncovered during a routine customer service interaction with its support team.

“Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability,” the supplier said in a statement.

Cisco warned that both physical and virtual versions of SEG – regardless of how they are configured – are affected.

Besides applying Cisco’s patch, most defenders can quickly confirm any attempted exploit by combing their SEG mail_logs for suspicious SQL statements. The presence of entries in the output may serve as an indicator of compromise (IoC), but according to Cisco, all users should additionally note that given CVE-2026-76461 opens up root privileges, an opsec-conscious threat actor could delete these.

“A root shell from a crafted email is about as bad as it gets, and the CVSS [base 9.8] score almost undersells it,” said Gunter Ollmann, chief technology officer at Cobalt, a supplier of penetration testing services. “Email gateways have to read untrusted content from anyone on the internet by design, then make trust decisions about it. That's exactly the kind of position attackers look for.”

Ollman said the rather more worrying aspect was the fact that attackers could wipe their IoCs. “If your detection strategy leans on matching known IoCs after the fact, you may have already missed the intrusion,” he said. “This is a good argument for putting more weight on behavioural and network-level detection around these devices, not just signature checks.”

Perimeter products targeted

The disclosure of CVE-2026-76461 comes hot on the heels of the discovery of other vulnerabilities discovered in Cisco perimeter products, in this case its Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) software.

The first of these, CVE-2026-20079 enables an unauthenticated, remote attacker to bypass authentication and execute script files on the affected system to gain root access. The second, CVE-2026-20316, enables an unauthenticated, remote attacker to log in to an affected device with a low-privileged account and potentially to access sensitive data.

According to an investigation conducted by Cisco’s Talos threat research unit, two distinct exploitation clusters have been detected. One of these clusters, attributed to a group Cisco tracks as UAT-11823, ultimately led to the deployment of a variant of the Cyclops Blink malware.

Cyclops Blink has been extensively used by the Russian state APT most commonly known as Sandworm – once described by Mandiant as one of the “most brazen” nation-state threats around.

“Perimeter security appliances need the same ongoing scrutiny as any other internet-facing application, not a patch cycle tied to change windows … Assume active probing against unpatched, reachable instances is already happening,” noted Ollman.

title: Capita doesn’t get to ‘walk away from’ civil service pension mess, says minister
raw_text:
The UK government will force Capita to fix the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) before any final decision can be made on insourcing the scheme, a minister has said.

In a Westminster Hall debate, the CSPS debacle was referred to as a “national scandal” by MPs.  

Responding to questions and troubling stories from MPs about constituents – former civil servants or their spouses – struggling financially, Sally Jameson MP, parliamentary secretary in the Cabinet Office, said: “[Capita] does not just walk away from this.”

Jameson was repeatedly asked about government plans to insource the scheme, already revealed in an earlier statement, although without a timeline. 

Capita went into CSPS contract unprepared

The CSPS contract transferred from MyCSP to Capita in December 2025, after being awarded in 2023. Despite having two years to prepare for it, in the month following Capita’s takeover, amid delays and problems, an HM Revenue & Customs troubleshooter was brought in to lead an “urgent recovery plan”.

Disaster after disaster has now prompted the government to make the decision to bring the service in-house, but no timeline has been given. What is now clear is the government won’t let Capta flee without fixing a scheme it will inevitably lose.

A Cabinet Office spokesperson recently told Computer Weekly that the government is “actively shaping a long-term strategy to bring the pension scheme back in-house” – a statement repeated by Jameson. But there is still uncertainty among members of the scheme, the trade union and MPs about what this means.

In the debate, Jameson declared her support for the government’s plan for the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation, but made clear that Capita cannot just walk away, leaving a mess.

“I want Capita to pay for their mistakes, not the taxpayers to pay for their mistakes. They don’t get to just walk away and do nothing about it,” she told MPs. “They need to pay for this, they need to get everyone their pensions, and then we’ll look at what needs to be done in terms of the viability of the scheme long term.”

Since it took over the contract from previous supplier MyCSP in December 2025, Capita has failed to meet its delivery promises and left claimants in severe financial difficulties. The company has admitted it is set to lose money on the contract, with pressure mounting on Capita, which is heavily reliant on public sector business, due to the government’s current insourcing plans combined with its much-publicised failures.

Jameson added: “We stood on a manifesto as a Labour government to have the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation. I am personally committed to that. I’ve said in this house before that I think that’s a priority for this [CSPS] scheme, but we can only do it when we make sure that it’s in the interest of the members. We’ve got to make sure that there is no disruption. We’ve got to do it in the smoothest and quickest way.”

The Westminster Hall debate was secured by Ian Byrne, MP for Liverpool West Derby. Opening the debate, he described the botched scheme as “the failure of outsourcing laid bare”. He called for details on the recovery, compensation for those affected and accountability for those responsible.

About 30 MPs spoke during the debate.

title: Splunk Conf 26: Splunk hopes to build confidence in agentic AI
raw_text:
Mere days after some of the most prominent “big AI” advocates went on record to warn of an existential threat to humanity arising from unchecked AI development, Splunk leadership made improving trust in agentic AI the headline topic at its annual .Conf customer event in Denver, Colorado.

Taking to the keynote stage, Jeetu Patel, chief product officer and president at Cisco, set the ball rolling by reflecting on the momentous change that has dominated the technology industry since the dawn of the agentic era in the autumn of 2024.

“We have squarely moved now from the era of chatbots to the world of agents, conducting tasks for us almost fully autonomously,” said Patel, who urged the audience to think of agents not as tools but as teammates.

Patel described four key changes underpinning the rapid growth of agentic AI. First, he said, “inference is the new workload”. Chatbot infrastructure consumption was spiky and ultimately, gated by a human’s capacity to engage – even power users weren’t putting too much strain on the underlying infrastructure, but now, agents are working 24-7, spawning more workloads for other agents almost continuously, so demand patterns are now higher and more consistent.

“In February this year, the tokens consumed by agents for the first time exceeded the total consumed by humans, which is wild,” said Patel. Seven months later, agents consume five times as many tokens, and since very few humans could currently be described as power users, this will only increase.

Second, he said, “agents are the new workforce”. This year, claimed Patel, 60% of global AI compute capacity will be put towards compute, with billions – maybe trillions – of agents using over five times more network bandwidth than humans, and maintaining visibility into the network to control their behaviour is becoming critical.

“Agents are like teenagers,” said Patel – they are intelligent, fearless and have poor judgement. They need to be monitored, and any drift in behaviour needs to be corrected in real time. That requires a fair amount of emphasis on visibility, as Patel observed, “you can’t fix what you can’t see”.

Third, he said, “tokens are the new currency”. The cost of tokens in the agentic world is in danger of getting out of control as fast-moving agents get chatty with one another in a way that humans talking to chatbots could never mentally sustain.

As a result, said Patel, we should anticipate more emphasis on open source and open weight AI models, and greater reliance on inferencing at the network edge, not in the hyperscale datacentre. Patel predicted those building out inferencing infrastructure will start to embrace a hybrid model, and while hyperscalers will remain a strong area of growth, organisations will build capacity in on-prem datacentres and even desktop computers.

Finally, “control is the new moat”, said Patel. We now live in a “post-Mythos world” where safety and security have become ironclad necessities, and all of the assumptions people had previously made about AI security are changing.

The bottom line, he said, is that every agentic action is simultaneously a routing challenge, a trust decision and a telemetry event. This is specifically why, Patel claimed, Splunk and Cisco created a vertically integrated, full stack platform, from silicon and photonics, up to network, compute, data, models, and AI apps and agents, with observability and security present at every level so that when the worst happens – whether that’s a technical outage or a cyber breach – detection and investigation becomes child’s play, and resources can be directed to remediation.

Ultimately, said Patel, this means organisations will be able to run agentic AI in confidence. He described a “world class, best of breed” observability proposition giving visibility into agent activity, application runtime, model performance and infrastructure utilisation; an agentic security operations centre (SOC) with the ability to process and understand every security event; and telemetry correlated from multiple domains, federated and analysed at lower cost, and unlocked for model training and agentic action.

This comes together in Cisco Cloud Control, which was unveiled at Cisco Live back in June and became available to US customers at the end of August. Patel described it as centralised control plane based on an agent-first operational model.

“Delivering digital resilience starts with Splunk. This is one of the most strategic acquisitions we [Cisco] ever made. If we were to do it again, I probably could be tricked into paying more for it,” said Patel.

title: UK, US and Netherlands warn of Iranian state spyware campaign
raw_text:
Iranian state hackers are targeting dissidents, activists and journalists with spyware capable of tracking their movements, GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned.

The Iranian spearphishing campaign has targeted people around the world, according to alerts from the UK, the Netherlands and the US.

Iranian cyber attackers have used social engineering techniques to persuade people to download files containing hidden malware that infects Windows-based devices.

The malware, identified as Chosen Brick, has been used to target individuals in the UK, the US and the Netherlands since at least 2025.

Personal information leaked

Once deployed, the malware enables Iranian state cyber attackers to collect information about a target’s contacts, emails and social media messages.

The personal details of victims have been published on pro-Iranian leak sites, potentially putting the personal safety of victims at risk.

According to UK intelligence assessments, Iran is almost certainly using cyber attacks to repress individuals seen as a threat to the regime.

In some cases, Iranian intelligence services have plotted to kidnap or conduct lethal operations against people they perceive as a threat outside of Iran.

Social engineering attack

Attackers contact victims through social media platforms and messaging services, such as WhatsApp, Telegram and Instagram, to build a rapport before tricking them into downloading the malware.

The attackers have deep knowledge of the target and often purport to be an individual known to them or pose as technical support from the social media platform.

They use their relationship with the victim to persuade them to download what appear to be legitimate files.

Malicious files have been disguised as artificial intelligence video-generating software Pictory, Norton Antivirus, messaging app Telegram, or password management tool KeePass. In other cases, malicious files have been disguised as MRI scan results.

The malware has the capability to download additional malware files to the infected machine, but has so far not been observed trying to spread to other machines.

It can be tasked with capturing the content of screens, enabling a microphone to capture audio, or capturing Telegram and WhatsApp data from browsers.

It can also delete files, steal the content of emails and wipe the infected computer system.

Paul Chichester, NCSC director of operations, said the UK would continue to call out malicious cyber activity by the Iranian state.

“The details of this cyber campaign reveal how Iran ruthlessly uses digital surveillance in pursuit of its aim to repress critics of the regime, stealing emails and messages and accessing devices,” he added.

title: The UK AI Strategy: Reorganisation is not delivery
raw_text:
On 17 July 2024, the King's Speech committed the UK government to bring forward binding regulation on the handful of companies developing the most powerful artificial intelligence (AI) models.

As I write, that commitment is 790 days old. It has not been delivered. It has not been withdrawn. It was simply absent from this year's legislative programme.

Interestingly, the state opening of Parliament on 13 May 2026 made no reference to artificial intelligence at all - not to an AI Bill, not to frontier model oversight, not to the promise made two years earlier.

The Regulating for Growth Bill appeared once, as a general measure to reduce the burden of unnecessary regulation through innovation. In July, the House of Commons Library recorded the position matter-of-factly. Such legislation, it noted, "has not yet been forthcoming".

This is how commitments end in UK government. Not with a decision, announced and defended in the House of Commons, but with an omission that nobody has to explain. A withdrawn commitment invites debate. A commitment that fails to appear in the next programme just slips away.

The UK's AI machinery moved instead

The contrast with the past eight weeks is hard to miss.

On 20 July, Kanishka Narayan was appointed minister of state for AI, a joint Cabinet Office and Department for Business and Trade (DBT) post covering AI strategy, the AI Taskforce, the AI Security Institute, and public sector adoption.

The following day, a government statement disbanded the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology altogether. An AI Taskforce was created at the centre of government. The Department for Culture, Media and Sport took on responsibility for digital foundations and transformation. DBT absorbed science and innovation and was renamed.

“Britain now has more AI machinery than at any point in its history, and the same number of binding obligations on the companies building frontier models as it had in July 2024, which is none”

Alan W. Brown

That is a substantial reorganisation, and parts of it are welcome. I have argued for several years that AI coordination belongs at the centre of government rather than in a sponsoring department, and this moves in that direction. But reorganisation is not delivery.

Britain now has more AI machinery than at any point in its history, and the same number of binding obligations on the companies building frontier models as it had in July 2024, which is none.

What the record shows

So, what’s going on? Since April I have tracked government progress against the 25 specific recommendations in my book, Making AI work for Britain, through a public scorecard, UK AI Watch. Each recommendation is rated against documented policy activity, and every rating is published with its evidence.

The position today is zero on track, 13 partially in place, and 12 not started. In five months, exactly one recommendation has moved, and it moved because of the July reorganisation rather than because anything was delivered.

A second finding is more revealing than the scorecard. The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard requires central government departments and public-facing arm's-length bodies to publish records of the algorithmic tools they use in consequential decisions.

The repository now holds 152 records from 38 organisations, which sounds like a scheme in good health. But look at who is publishing. Now, 16 of those 38 are local councils, police forces, and devolved bodies for which the standard is entirely voluntary. The volunteers are flattering the compliance figures of the duty holders.

The case for the defence

The UK government's position, set out in February 2025 and unchanged since, is that most AI systems are best regulated at the point of use by the expert regulators who already understand each sector. From that perspective, the absence of an AI Act is not a failure but a deliberate and defensible choice, and the UK has avoided saddling the emerging AI industry with compliance costs while the technology is still moving.

It’s a reasonable position but becoming harder to defend. This week, the Joint Committee on Human Rights published a report describing the current point-of-deployment framework as ill-equipped to deter preventable harms, and calling for a single statutory regulator with the power to sanction wrongdoing. It also notes that the AI Security Institute operates on a voluntary basis with no statutory power, a point that doesn’t sit well with the government's confidence in the current approach.

Nor is the UK’s record uniformly thin. The £100m Sovereign AI R&D scheme launched on 31 August deliberately removes turnover and track record requirements so that smaller companies can compete for government contracts, which is precisely the kind of supplier diversity that public procurement usually crushes. Meanwhile, sovereign compute capacity has grown substantially. Similarly, the AI Security Institute has shown it has real international standing.

The problem is not that ministers chose sector-led regulation. It is that they promised something else, in the King's Speech, and then neither did it nor said they had stopped. One is a disagreement about policy. The other is a failure to be open about it.

A test worth applying

The Sovereign AI scheme illustrates the problems with this approach. Announcing it, the UK government confirmed that successful companies "will also keep the intellectual property they create". No data portability terms, architecture documentation requirements, or funded transition arrangements have been published alongside it. The state is buying capability it will not own and has not secured the means to leave.

So here is a test that any minister, select committee, or interested party can apply, and doesn’t require a complex scorecard.

Take any AI commitment government has made in the past few years. Establish the date it was made, whether the specific thing promised now exists, and if not, whether a minister has stood up and said it will not happen. The commitments that survive that test are policy. The rest are announcements with no implementation plan.

On the evidence of the past few years, Britain has been producing rather more announcements than policy. Without a decision to change that, the gap will widen.

Alan W. Brown is Professor of Digital Economy at the University of Exeter Business School and research director at the Digital Policy Alliance. He is the author of Making AI Work for Britain (London Publishing Partnership, 2026).

title: UK Atomic Energy Authority readies US artificial intelligence collaboration
raw_text:
The UK Atomic Energy Authority (UKAEA) has announced plans to look at how it can work with the US Department of Energy’s Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) to deliver federated supercomputing for fusion research.

During the Global Fusion Policy Summit held in London, UKAEA and PPPL signed a joint declaration of intent to explore linking UKAEA’s Sunrise AI supercomputer with PPPL’s Stellar-AI platform through a partnership known as the Sunrise–Stellar-AI Federation.

The aim is to enable researchers on both sides of the Atlantic to train artificial intelligence (AI) models on results from both national laboratories and develop AI tools for future fusion power plants, drawing on experiments completed using UKAEA’s Mast Upgrade facility in Oxfordshire and PPPL’s NSTX-U facility in New Jersey. 

The federation will mean both advanced computers will be used to train the same AI models, which need large volumes of high-quality data to make accurate predictions, shortening the design cycle for future fusion power plants.

Joe Milnes, executive director for engineering and computing at UKAEA, said: “Fusion is one of the great scientific and engineering challenges of our time. To solve these challenges, fusion needs partnerships.”

The planned collaboration will also look at developing digital twins of both facilities, providing detailed virtual copies of a real fusion machine, supported by regular data from fusion experiments. This could help researchers test changes and predict how the machine will behave in software before applying experiments to hardware.

Shantenu Jha, head of computational science at PPPL, said: “Our goal is to let models and experiments move freely between the two systems. We will turn a collection of supercomputers into a single engine for fusion discovery.”

Read more UKAEA stories

  • Nuclear Fusion HPC: We speak to UKAEA director for computing programmes, Rob Akers, about the new Sunrise AI supercomputer for nuclear fusion research and development.
  • UK Atomic Energy Authority readies fusion simulation AI supercomputer: The AMD Epyc and Instinct-powered Dell hardware will deliver 6.74 exaflops to power digital twins to support nuclear fusion research.

Researchers will also examine how to move computing jobs smoothly between platforms, which use different hardware, so scientists can pick the right supercomputing platform for each problem.

Jonathan Menard, chief scientist at PPPL, said: “By federating the Sunrise and Stellar-AI computer platforms, we can train AI on data from two leading fusion facilities, test ideas across two of the most capable computing systems in the world that are designed for fusion research, and accelerate the path to a compact fusion power plant.”

According to UKAEA and PPPL, when different facilities are combined, researchers can develop more powerful machine learning models that better capture the underlying physics and help accelerate future fusion projects, including the UK’s Spherical Tokamak for Energy Production and US concepts such as PPPL’s Spherical Tokamak Advanced Reactor.

The federation also wants to develop the next generation of fusion and AI experts through training, workshops, research opportunities and other international collaborations.

Rob Akers, director of computing programmes and senior fellow at UKAEA, said: “UKAEA and PPPL would draw on experimental data from two world-leading fusion machines, using simulation to fill the gaps and extend those datasets into regimes we have yet to explore. Together, we can develop digital twins of both machines to support the design of future fusion power plants, creating models of spherical tokamaks that are more predictive, more actionable, and ultimately more useful to fusion engineers.”

title: Data dive: The revolving door between Whitehall and big tech
raw_text:
What do a former head of GCHQ, the author of the MoD’s Defence AI Strategy, a former prime minister and the founder of the Government Digital Service (GDS) have in common? They all left very senior roles in the UK government and public sector for jobs with IT and artificial intelligence (AI) suppliers that supply the UK government and public sector.

Those are the findings of a Computer Weekly analysis that mapped the revolving door between Whitehall and public sector technology suppliers. The dataset holds 63 moves since 2010 – a small number, but one that captures only the very top echelons of the civil service, and the visible tip of a larger flow that no public register records.

In this article, we outline what the data shows, which suppliers attract the most former officials, who some of those officials are, and why 63 is best read as a low figure that becomes much higher when other levels are considered.

What we counted

The analysis traces 63 moves between the UK public sector and 20 IT, cloud and AI suppliers from 2010 to 2026. Every record carries a public source – a Business Appointment Rules decision, a Companies House filing, a civil service organogram or a press report – so each can be checked.

The concentration is striking. Palantir accounts for nine of the 63 moves – more than any other supplier. Deloitte follows with eight, then Anthropic and Public Digital with five each, and BAE Systems, Microsoft, IBM, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Quantexa with four apiece.

The door mostly swings one way. Sixty of the 63 moves run from government to supplier. Just three run the other way, among them Craig Suckling, who moved from AWS to become the government’s chief data officer in 2024, and Doug Gurr, the former Amazon UK boss who became interim chair of the Competition and Markets Authority in 2025.

The names behind the numbers

The most concentrated cluster sits at Quantexa, the London data analytics firm whose software maps fraud and money-laundering networks for banks and governments. Jeremy Fleming ran GCHQ, the UK’s signals intelligence agency, from 2017 to 2023; he is now an advisory board member at Quantexa. He is not the only former public official there. Matthew Gould, who led NHSX – the NHS’s digital and data unit – through the pandemic, went to Quantexa too, as did Lucy Frazer, a Cabinet minister until 2024, and Franck Petitgas, Rishi Sunak’s chief business adviser.

The defence side of the door is just as direct. Laurence Lee served as the Ministry of Defence’s second permanent secretary from 2021 to 2023, overseeing its digital and AI work and co-writing the Defence AI Strategy. In 2024, he became geostrategic adviser to Palantir’s chief executive. In late 2025, Palantir agreed its largest ever UK defence deal, a £240m no-bid contract.

The examples extend beyond data and defence. Rishi Sunak, who as prime minister pitched Britain as an AI superpower, now advises Microsoft and Anthropic. And the people who built Gov.uk – Mike Bracken, Tom Loosemore, Ben Terrett and James Stewart, the founding team of the Government Digital Service – went on to found and lead Public Digital, a consultancy whose clients include HM Revenue & Customs.

The methodology behind the data

The dataset draws on public sources. The Business Appointment Rules registers – ACOBA’s decisions for the most senior officials and the quarterly departmental releases for the grades just below – supply 48 of the 63 moves. Public trade press supplies the remaining 15, most of them the AWS and Amazon records that predate the individual ACOBA publications. Companies House officer records and the twice-yearly civil service organograms provide the surrounding context – the supplier directors and the pool of senior civil servants the moves were drawn from.

The analysis is bounded at Senior Civil Service (SCS) level and above – deputy director and up, plus ministers and special advisers. Below that line, the rules do not require publication, and nothing is recorded. 

The tip of the iceberg

The Business Appointment Rules apply only to the most senior grades. A former official one grade below – a Grade 6 or Grade 7 programme lead, or a police or NHS manager outside the SCS system entirely – can move to a supplier without any public register recording the move.

An investigation by The Nerve reported in April 2026 that Palantir had recruited 32 UK government and public sector officials since 2012, most of them below the senior threshold the rules cover. A simple search on LinkedIn for “government Palantir” surfaces former Metropolitan Police and Cabinet Office staff on the firm’s books – people who sit beneath the register.

None of this makes the 63 wrong. It makes the 63 what is publicly countable, and the true flow larger. The rules draw the line near the top, and the top is where the fewest people are.

Good for the suppliers – good for the public?

The 63 moves are, in almost every case, lawful and cleared under the rules that apply. One case stands out: Norman Driskell, the Home Office’s chief digital officer, joined Amazon in 2017 without the required clearance, it was reported at that time.

But the direction of the flow carries a question. The people who wrote procurement specifications, ran public data policy and led digital transformation now sit, in a growing number of cases, on the other side of the table – employed by, or advising, the suppliers that sell to the departments they once served. That flow is self-evidently good for the suppliers, or it would not happen. Whether it is good for the public is a different question, and one the current transparency rules do not let the public answer below the senior grades.

Key definitions

SCS – Senior Civil Service, which covers the top grades of the civil service, from deputy director up. 

ACOBA – the Advisory Committee on Business Appointments, which cleared (and published) moves for the most senior officials until October 2025. 

Business Appointment Rules – the rules governing what former ministers and senior civil servants may do after leaving government. 

GDS – the Government Digital Service, which built Gov.uk. 

GCHQ – the UK’s signals intelligence agency.

title: Transformers: More than meets the eye in datacentre grid connection
raw_text:
In the relentless expansion of hyperscale computing, where racks packed with graphics processing units (GPUs) can demand more than 100kW each, the spotlight often falls on flashy silicon and sophisticated algorithms. But behind the scenes a foundational piece of electrical infrastructure quietly dictates the success or failure of the digital economy – the power transformer.

These devices, which efficiently step voltage up or down, stabilise supplies, and minimise losses, have become strategic enablers for the AI boom. For modern datacentres, especially those chasing grid-scale capacity and renewable integration, advanced transformers represent far more than utility hardware. They are the linchpin for reliable, sustainable scaling.

Nowhere is this shift more evident than in large European projects that use direct high-voltage connections. One notable example is a campus near Berlin that launched with substantial connected capacity through massive super-grid transformers linked straight to the transmission network and so avoided straining local distribution networks used by communities and businesses. Such deployments highlight how thoughtful power architecture can support explosive growth while aligning with environmental goals.

Understanding transformers: principles and evolution

The basic operating principle of the transformer dates back to Michael Faraday’s 1831 experiments with electromagnetic induction. Alternating current in a primary winding generates a changing magnetic field in an iron core, which induces voltage in a secondary winding. By adjusting the ratio of turns between windings, engineers can precisely control voltage levels, stepping it up for efficient long-distance transmission or down for safe utilisation.

Power losses during transmission are governed by Joule’s law, expressed as P = I2R, where P is power loss, I is current, and R is electrical resistance, and in which losses escalate dramatically with current – it specifically calculates the rate at which electrical energy is converted into heat as current flows through a conductor. 

High-voltage transmission reduces current for the same power level, to slash resistive losses. Traditional distribution transformers typically connect at 30kV - 110kV on the primary side. In contrast, super-grid or transmission-level transformers handle 380kV or higher directly from the high-voltage backbone, stepping down to medium-voltage levels (around 30 kV) for datacentre use.

These units are typically filled with synthetic oil for optimal insulation and cooling. They are physically imposing, engineered for decades of continuous operation under varying loads, and critical for handling the dynamic demands of modern facilities. In datacentres, transformers supply everything from cooling systems and uninterruptible power supply (UPS) units to server racks, including support for emerging high-voltage DC architectures like 800V systems.

Even minor efficiency gains here compound significantly. Inefficiencies manifest as excess heat, driving up cooling demands and overall Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE). For AI workloads with extreme densities, optimising this layer directly impacts energy costs and carbon footprints.

Limitations of conventional approaches

Global datacentre electricity demand is forecast to triple by 2030, fuelled by cloud computing and especially AI training and inference clusters that can consume tens of megawatts continuously. Traditional electrical designs, built around multiple transformation stages from lower-voltage distribution networks, struggle with the scale, efficiency, and resilience required.

Super-grid transformers address these constraints by connecting directly at transmission voltages. This reduces transformation stages, boosts capacity, and improves operational reliability. Automated voltage regulation provides tighter control across the entire campus. Higher primary voltages also enhance grid resilience, and often diminish the need for extensive on-site backup generation.

The shift is not merely technical. It responds to the broader pressures of soaring energy prices, regulatory decarbonisation mandates, and the physical limits of local grids. Many regions face constraints where adding large loads could strain local distribution networks, and affect businesses and residents. Direct transmission-level connections bypass these issues, delivering a competitive edge for AI infrastructure development.

Spotlight on high-capacity European deployments

A compelling illustration comes from developments in Germany, where a major campus near Berlin has deployed two exceptionally large 185MVA super-grid transformers. Connected directly to the 380kV transmission network operated by 50Hertz, the site initially offers 300MVA of capacity, with clear pathways to scale toward 500MVA. This represents one of the most ambitious grid integrations for a European datacentre to date.

The design incorporates full 2N redundancy – dual independent paths for critical systems – that targets 99.999% (five nines) availability. Paired with on-site substation infrastructure, it enables seamless scaling for customers. Importantly, the high-voltage approach avoids burdening local distribution networks to preserve capacity for surrounding communities and businesses. This kind of forward-thinking infrastructure positions locations like Berlin as attractive hubs for the AI economy.

Enabling a zero-generator future

Many datacentres have traditionally depended on diesel generators for backup power. While effective for rapid response, these systems introduce drawbacks. They have high embedded carbon, bring fuel storage and logistics challenges, require ongoing maintenance, release emissions that impact air quality, and are under regulatory scrutiny.

Advanced grid connections to robust, “stiff” transmission networks, which are  characterised by meshed topology, multiple infeed points, and significant renewable contributions, offer compelling alternatives. In regions with strong onshore wind resources, for instance, direct feeds can deliver exceptional stability and uptime. Combined with redundant architectures, this can make standby diesel generators optional rather than mandatory, to support customer preferences for higher sustainability without compromising resilience.

Facilities committing to 100% certified renewable energy further amplify these benefits. The result is a more environmentally aligned operation that also reduces operational complexity and long-term costs.

Transformers as the foundation for tomorrow’s energy hubs

The deployment of super-grid transformers in projects like the Berlin example serves as a blueprint for the industry. By combining massive high-voltage connections, redundancy, renewable alignment, and optional generation strategies, operators can reconcile rapid AI growth with sustainability imperatives.

The future of artificial intelligence will hinge not only on chips and code but on the intelligent management of electrons. Transformers, re-engineered for the demands of the super-grid and AI era, stand as quiet enablers of that progress. They are essential infrastructure that makes scalable, responsible computing not just possible, but inevitable.

Mike Golding is SVP design & build at Virtus Datacentres

title: CW@60: Don’t forget your toothbrush - guarding sources, exposing the secret state
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

Britain’s most secret court had just gone into a secret session and I hurriedly left the press benches, grabbing my coat and my rucksack.

Outside in the corridor I fumbled for my phone. As I was rummaging in my bag a woman appeared from nowhere. A court official, or a member of the security services, I couldn’t be sure. I panicked. Had I left my phone in court during a secret hearing? Would I be called up before the judge for contempt?

Fortunately, I was not guilty of spying. Unlike MI5, MI6 and GCHQ, which the court found had unlawfully collected data on the activities of the campaigning group, Privacy International, and kept it stored in an overlooked part of their IT system. A huge data protection failure.

During the same court hearings, a senior director of GCHQ had to retract his witness statement after giving incorrect evidence on oath from behind a screen. But this was far from my first experience of the courts.

A confidential source

I became interested in justice and the law three months into my first job as a reporter on The Engineer magazine in 1989, when I received an injunction from a computer software company and subsequently found myself in the High Court, facing demands to disclose the identity of a confidential source.

Bill Goodwin

Back in court, I found myself reporting on US attempts to extradite young men, often neurodivergent, accused of hacking their way into government computer systems. Gary McKinnon, Lauri Love, and latterly Julian Assange were judged to be at risk of suicide in the harsh US prison systems and ultimately spared.

Mass data collection

Advances in technology have allowed private sector companies and government agencies to collect data on individuals on a mass scale, raising uncomfortable questions about people’s privacy rights.

With NBC, based on leaked documents, we exposed how Facebook had cynically backtracked on promises to protect users’ privacy for profit, and betrayed developers that built apps for its platform.

With Correctiv in Germany and Solomon in Greece, we showed how the European Union’s police agency, Europol, stored vast amounts of sensitive data on a system with significant security and privacy flaws that failed to meet EU data protection law.

And we analysed thousands of leaked emails with Byline Times, which revealed that the former MI6 chief, Sir Richard Dearlove, joined with hard Brexit-supporters and White House advisers to secretly lobby the government to drop the Chinese company Huawei from the UK’s telecoms network – against the advice of MI5 and GCHQ.

I have not been asked to identify my sources at Computer Weekly. Apart from once. I was phoned by a detective from Scotland Yard’s Computer Crime Unit, enquiring about the source of a story about a recruitment agency.

The company had left its clients’ CVs unprotected for anyone to download on the internet – if you knew the right URL. After legal advice, I declined. The agency retaliated by filing a complaint to the Press Complaints Commission but lost on every point.

Since the Snowden revelations in 2013, the government moved to place previously secret surveillance powers on a statutory footing, by avowing their existence, culminating in the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. The Investigatory Powers Tribunal has played a role in holding government departments to account.

A surreal experience

Computer Weekly continues to report on the implications of mass data collection by the state and private sector companies for privacy, data protection and justice.

It was a surreal experience attending hearings of the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) recently, and hearing my own case being talked about by barristers and judges.

The IPT cases have revealed shocking and unlawful police and MI5 surveillance of BBC and other journalists working in Northern Ireland - not least Barry McCaffrey and Trevor Birney, who were targeted for exposing police collusion with paramilitaries - as law enforcement agencies sought their communications data to identify their confidential sources.

Jon Boutcher, head of the Police Service of Northern Ireland, says there have been significant changes to practice and policy since then and that the Home Office has remedied defects in the communications data code of practice to offer journalists greater protection.

Does that mean the risks to journalists and their sources are over? I don’t think so. The next battleground will be encrypted communications, as governments push for back-door access to encrypted services, that journalists, human rights workers, and people at risk in oppressive regimes rely on for their safety and the safety of their contacts.

title: CW@60: Navigating the waves and storms of technological change
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

I first encountered computing at primary school, when ZX81s began appearing in classrooms. It felt novel, and slightly mysterious, but most importantly, full of possibility.

Even now I can remember how proud I was when I wrote a programme to generate my Christmas thank you letters from a file of names and gifts. I am not sure my grandparents appreciated the combination of technical challenges overcome and productivity improvement, but I was hooked.

By the time I started work, inter-office memos were still being typed and placed in brown envelopes to be sent around the organisation. Early electronic messaging then arrived, although it seemed rather odd to send a digital message to somebody sitting only a few metres away.

New technology can look underwhelming when judged only against what came before. Its significance often becomes clear once people use it in ways that were not obvious at the outset.

Waves and storms

Not all technological change arrives in the same way. I tend to think of it as a sequence of waves and storms.

In this particular metaphor, waves accelerate a direction in which organisations are already travelling. For example, cloud computing made infrastructure and software easier to access and scale; agile changed how many organisations designed and delivered technology.

Storms are different, altering the course completely. And for me, three stand out - the commercial internet, the smartphone, and now, generative AI.

I must admit that when the iPhone first appeared, I was not immediately converted. Its battery life compared poorly with a dependable Nokia and the signal didn’t always inspire confidence. Judged simply as a telephone, it looked rather imperfect - but that missed the point. It changed what people expected to be able to do, wherever they were.

Generative AI feels like another such moment. Among all the excitement, there is just as much anxiety – both of which are contributing to the noise surrounding it. It did not appear from nowhere, though. The cloud, data and digital foundations built over the past decade made it possible. Waves can prepare the conditions for storms.

Making technology useful

Storms encourage a familiar mistake - assuming that because a technology can do something, it necessarily should.

The inter-office memo was slow, but the friction had value. You had to think about what you were asking, who needed to know and whether the message was worth sending. Email removed much of that friction. It also allowed us to communicate at enormous volume, but not always with better results.

“New technologies deserve curiosity, but not blind faith. You always need to look at the evidence, understand the context, and change course when circumstances demand it”

Maynard Williams

I may be wrong, but few people look at their inbox and conclude that the problem is a shortage of messages. AI presents a similar tension.

Believe me, I am not nostalgic for brown envelopes. The point is that how we use technology needs as much thought as the technology itself. Better tools do not remove the need for judgement. More often, they increase it.

Knowing enough to ask the right questions

A navigator still needs to know how to read a map, even when using GPS. It helps when the system fails, but also when the technology may be leading them astray.

Technology has become easier to use because more complexity is hidden from view. When I began programming, developers had to think directly about memory management. Much of that is now abstracted away. This is progress, but it can distance us from what a system is doing.

With generative AI, a basic understanding of models, prompts, data and token use can separate something useful from something expensive or unreliable.

I have a bias for action and testing ideas practically. So before building technology, I ask, what problem are we solving? What outcome do we expect? How will we know whether it worked?

I witnessed this recently while working with a financial services firm. The initial question was how AI could help manage parts of its technology operations. On paper, this looked sensible, but once we began prototyping and working through the details, it became clear that the bigger challenge lay elsewhere.

The more important question was how AI should fit into the enterprise architecture in the first place. That led them to think more broadly about how those capabilities should be designed into the technology estate, and what would be needed to support them. It was a useful reminder that the first question asked about AI is often not the most important one.

Admittedly, these questions are easily lost amid the excitement. Saying employees will be more productive or customers more satisfied is not enough. The hypothesis and measure should come before the technology, not afterwards.

Learning by doing

Technologists still need depth, but increasingly they need breadth too. Technical expertise cannot be separated from an understanding of the business, its customers and the people who will use what is built.

Leaders do not need to become software engineers, but they need enough technological understanding to ask sensible questions and assess the answers.

The people I have most admired throughout my career have retained a willingness to learn by doing. They remain curious, but not credulous. They try new tools, find their limits, and learn from the result.

That matters with AI. The aim is not to use it for its own sake, but to understand where it can improve a process, service or decision, and where it adds cost, risk or complexity.

The things that endure

I have been lucky to ride many waves of technological change during my career. The storms have been less comfortable, but also the most interesting. They are the moments when assumptions fall away and people have to learn again.

For all the excitement surrounding each new era of technology, the fundamentals are remarkably durable. We still design, build, test and ship code, simply with different tools and expectations.

People are equally constant. Relationships, trust, clear communication and common sense will resolve more technical problems than any single platform or methodology. People remember whether you supported the team and were honest when things went wrong. Our industry is smaller than it appears, and it has a long memory.

New technologies deserve curiosity, but not blind faith. You always need to look at the evidence, understand the context, and change course when circumstances demand it.

The tools have changed enormously since those first ZX81s. Curiosity, trust and common sense have proved rather more durable.

title: UK rolls out digital ID for alcohol sales
raw_text:
The hospitality and retail sectors will be empowered to adopt certified digital identification technology to verify legal alcohol purchases under new rules to be rolled out by the UK government.

Operating alongside – but not replacing – traditional physical forms of identity such as driving licences or passports, Westminster said the changes will make age checks quicker, easier and more secure for both customers and staff.

The changes to Section 182 of the 2003 Licensing Act come in the wake of a 2024 consultation in which 72% of respondents said that they supported the use of digital ID for age verification when buying alcoholic drinks.

The government said that although it would take time for businesses to adopt and accept digital IDs, the new system will ultimately prove a more convenient alternative to carrying a physical form of ID.

The government said that the simple act of showing a QR code or tapping a device on a compatible reader will confirm to staff that a customer is over 18 with more confidence than merely checking a physical document because, in the background, certified services will have already checked the ID is genuine and belongs to the person presenting it.

This will also serve to cut the risk to businesses of accidentally letting a fake or borrowed ID slip through the net.

Meanwhile, for customers, besides putting an end to worries over leaving your driving licence at home, the government claimed it will also improve personal security to a small extent by eliminating the need to hand over a physical ID showing personally identifiable information.

And when speed is often of the essence, both businesses and customers will benefit from more efficient service, whether in a supermarket at 5:30 on Christmas Eve, a packed pub on a Friday night, in a loud and dark nightclub, or during a break at a sporting event.

“From pubs and restaurants to music venues and festivals, licensed businesses carry out millions of age checks every year. It will remain an individual or business’ choice whether to use or adopt it, and physical ID will remain a valid way for customers to prove their age,” said digital government minister Stephanie Peacock.

“This groundbreaking change in the law will mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information such as your name or address just to prove your age, allowing everyone to feel safer on a night out.”

UKHospitality chief exec Allen Simpson added: “Introducing digital proof of age is a positive step for hospitality, providing greater flexibility and convenience for customers and businesses. 

“The roll-out of the voluntary digital proof of age will provide an easier experience for customers, allowing them to verify their age securely from their phones. We look forward to working with the government to ensure the roll-out of the scheme, with multiple supplier options available, is cost-efficient and not burdensome for the hospitality sector,” said Simpson.

Familiar faces

Similar services are already well in use across the UK as a means to help people verify their identify online to access services, and the new rules build on this existing certified technology from the likes of Yoti, which collaborated on a similar service for the Post Office in 2021.

Yoti co-founder and CEO Robin Tombs described the change in the law was a landmark moment for digital identity in Britain.

“We’re delighted that businesses in England and Wales can now start accepting apps like Yoti ID and Post Office EasyID as proof of age for alcohol sales,” he said. “It gives premises an additional way to carry out age checks while offering customers a convenient alternative to physical ID.”

Digital proof of age will have to be provided through a certified digital verification service listed on the statutory register on Gov.uk, which has been shown to meet relevant standards under the UK’s digital verification services trust framework. For now, digital proof of age will be separate from digital driving licences and Gov.uk Wallet, although in time it is hoped both these forms of ID will come in scope.

Crucially, shops and hospitality venues will not be forced to adopt any such digital identification system and can continue to use physical ID checks, said the government.

Read more about digital ID

  • While the government may have cancelled its digital ID scheme, challenges such as fragmented data, digital access to public services and public trust remain.
  • Back-to-front policy and a rushed launch destroyed public confidence, as Home Affairs Committee is sceptical government has capacity to implement the digital ID programme.
  • The King's Speech outlined plans for a Digital Access to Services Bill, establishing a legal framework for the use of digital identity, which has received mixed responses.

title: UK lawmakers call for new law to protect human rights from AI systems
raw_text:
British lawmakers are calling for a new law and a statutory oversight body to address the “serious threats” posed by artificial intelligence (AI) systems to people’s human rights.

Parliament’s Joint Committee on Human Rights said the UK needed stronger safeguards including a statutory AI oversight body and legislation to address the risks of AI.

The report’s publication follows calls from US AI leaders yesterday to slow down the pace of development of AI to give companies more time to focus on safety.

In recent weeks, incidents of AI going rogue, including a swarm of 700 AI agents created by OpenAI, collaborating to hack open source platform Hugging Face, have led to calls for greater scrutiny of AI.

The cross-party group of MPs and peers called for the government to take “immediate” action, including banning the most dangerous uses of AI, and to introduce strong sanctions against companies and organisations that damage human rights through their use of AI.

Alex Sobel, chair of the joint committee, said that AI was moving with such speed and complexity that its impact is hard to predict. “Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach that is fit for purpose,” he said.

Anthropic founder and CEO Dario Amodei has posted an essay on social media, urging a slow-down in the speed of development of AI models. “I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence,” he wrote, in a post supported by Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

His comments came after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon publicly resigned, warning that there was a global arms race underway in AI. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he wrote in a post on X.

Call for AI Bill

The cross-party committee is calling for the UK to bring forward an AI Bill, first announced in the King’s Speech in 2024, to regulate the development of powerful AI models.

It said that the rights of people in the UK were threatened by a lack of transparency over how AI systems were being used in decision-making and the lack of effective mechanisms to challenge decisions made by AI that have adverse effects on people.

The MPs and peers, in a 100-page report, call for the UK to create a statutory AI oversight body that would have the powers to test and evaluate high-risk uses of AI before they are deployed, and to prevent AI systems that pose “unacceptable” risks to human rights being deployed.

It would also have powers to investigate breaches of law and mandatory codes of conduct issued by the proposed oversight body, and to sanction any companies or individuals that fail to comply.

Companies that develop powerful AI models would be required to submit them for review, evaluation and testing to the AI Security Institute (AISI), which would also be placed on a statutory footing.

Significant risks

“The Hugging Face incident illustrates the significant risks that can arise from the newest and most advanced AI models, and legislation should address those risks on a precautionary basis with a view to avoiding harm,” the committee said.

The committee found that the current legal framework is fragmented, and leaves gaps which fail to address human rights risks. It said there was “insufficient transparency” over how AI systems are used in decision-making and a lack of effective mechanisms to challenge those decisions.

Organisations that deploy AI systems that could have significant impacts on individuals or groups should have an obligation to state that AI is being used, and to explain what it is being used for, the parliamentarians said.

Human-in-the-loop not enough

The report stated: “The mere presence of a ‘human in the loop’ would not be enough to show significant human involvement or intervention in AI decision-making. It should be necessary to show that the person is sufficiently informed and independent to be able to reach an objective view that has not been improperly influenced.”

Low-risk AI systems, used to automate simple tasks – for example, planning events or shopping – should be subject to fewer and less demanding legal requirements.

But high-risk practices, which could include AI systems that profile people to predict the likelihood of committing a criminal offence, infer emotions in the workplace, or use real-time biometric identification in public places, should be prohibited, subject to a public consultation.

Alex Sobel, who introduced a 10-minute rule bill last week to require the UK government to secure an international agreement to prevent the development of superintelligent AI, said individuals should be told when AI is used to make decisions about them.

“We also want to make sure that if something does go wrong, then avenues of redress will be available,” he added. “We need these protections now.”

The government last week rejected calls for an AI Kill Switch, proposed by Lib Dem peer Tim Clement-Jones as an amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill (CSRB), currently going through Parliament.

A government spokesperson told Computer Weekly, “Any future measures will be evidence-based and focused on the risks we need to address.”

What are the human rights risks of AI?

AI has the potential to be used in highly intrusive ways, according to the UK Parliament’s cross-party Joint Committee on Human Rights, including collecting personal data from individuals without their agreement or knowledge.

For example, between January 2025 and October 2025, around three million people would have had their faces scanned by police facial recognition technology.

“The availability of AI systems also increases the risk that individuals can be re-identified from apparently anonymous data, especially when they can draw on multiple datasets to allow the combination of different potentially identifying factors,” the report states.

The committee heard evidence that the abuse of AI systems, such as creating deepfake intimate images, can have a disproportionate impact on minority groups.

In other cases, individuals can face discrimination from biases in AI systems used by the public sector and private sector.

In one case, an Uber Eats driver could not log on for work because the AI facial recognition software used, which was worse at identifying black people, did not recognise him.

Durham Constabulary used an AI system to predict the risks of re-offending and to inform decisions about whether to prosecute people. The system was heavily weighted towards postcode and location, according to evidence heard by the committee.

Amazon withdrew an AI recruitment tool after it was found to discriminate against female applicants.

Lack of legal remedies

AI systems can be deployed to support decision-making with legal or other significant effects on individuals affected, the committee found in its 100-page report.

Lack of transparency by public bodies deploying AI could adversely affect the ability of affected individuals to challenge decisions by public bodies.

Even if individuals were made aware that AI was being used, they may not be provided with enough information to understand the basis of the output to mount an effective challenge.
